questions.title: How do the Fifth Circuit JMOL standard and the Federal Circuit’s substantial evidence review interact here?
questions.question_body: The opinion says it reviews denial of JMOL under Fifth Circuit law (de novo, reversing only if the evidence overwhelmingly favors one side) and also says infringement findings are reviewed for substantial evidence. I'm confused about which standard really drives the outcome: is the Federal Circuit applying the Fifth Circuit’s JMOL standard to assess whether substantial evidence supports the jury verdict, or are these two independent layers of review? How should I conceptualize the court’s task when it says it reverses because the verdict isn't supported by substantial evidence?

questions.title: Why can’t a post-ADC modeled PIM path satisfy the ’134 patent’s requirement that the receiver samples the interference-generating signals?
questions.question_body: For the ’134 patent, the court holds that limitation 1[a] requires the RF ADC to sample a passband that includes both the signals of interest and the interference-generating signals. Finesse’s expert mapped the interference-generating signals to a modeled PIM path that, per the record, is generated downstream (after the RF ADC). Is the timing/location of signal generation dispositive as a matter of claim scope (i.e., interference-generating signals must pre-exist at the sampling stage), or could a model or estimate be considered part of the ‘received signals’? What claim language or construction forecloses using a modeled signal created later in the pipeline to meet the ‘interference generating signals’ limitation at the sampling step?

questions.title: When does contradictory expert testimony become legally insufficient to support a verdict?
questions.question_body: The court relies on Johns Hopkins v. Datascope to hold that Finesse’s infringement case (for the ’134 patent) failed because the expert gave inconsistent mappings (sometimes tying ‘interference generating signals’ to the modeled PIM path generated after ADC, other times referencing x1/x2 without clearly mapping them to the claim terms). What is the doctrinal threshold for deeming expert testimony too contradictory or confusing to constitute substantial evidence? Is it enough that there’s internal inconsistency, or must there be an affirmative concession that defeats a required element? How much latitude does a jury have to reconcile inconsistencies versus the appellate court declaring the testimony inadequate as a matter of law?

questions.title: Did the ’775 patent’s prosecution history clearly disclaim two-signal implementations when the claims were amended to ‘three signals S1, S2 and S3’?
questions.question_body: Appellants argued that changing ‘two or three signals’ to ‘three signals’ surrendered two-signal embodiments (like Filipovic). The Federal Circuit rejected clear and unambiguous disavowal, emphasizing the patentee’s focus on passive (not active) IMPs and a construction requiring only ‘three separately identifiable signals,’ not necessarily three unique inputs. How do we reconcile the text ‘three signals S1, S2 and S3’ with the court’s acceptance that they need not be unique? What features of the amendment/arguments fell short of Cont’l Circuits’ clear-disavowal standard, and what are examples of language that would have constituted a clear surrender in this context?

questions.title: For the ’775 patent, must the patentee prove each of the seven specific third-order multiplications, or can three distinct products ‘stand in’ for seven?
questions.question_body: The claim recites generating an n-th order ICS by ‘digitally multiplying and filtering’ seven specified third-order combinations of S1, S2, and S3. Finesse’s expert identified only three distinct products in Nokia’s documents (e.g., x1·|x1|·|x1|; x1·x1·x2′; x1·|x2|·|x2|), and the court held that no reasonable jury could find all seven from this. Is there any doctrinal basis (e.g., equivalence, repeated operations, or signal identity) that would allow three distinct multiplications to satisfy a claim that literally enumerates seven? Also, do operations involving complex conjugates and moduli qualify as the ‘digitally multiplying’ of S1, S2, S3 as-claimed, or does the presence of conjugate/modulus transform them into different ‘signals’ that break one-to-one mapping to the seven listed terms?

questions.title: Was the ‘uniqueness’ argument about S1, S2, S3 preserved for JMOL, and how does Rule 50(a) waiver apply here?
questions.question_body: The district court said Appellants waived the argument that S1, S2, and S3 must be ‘unique’ by not raising it at Rule 50(a). On appeal, the Federal Circuit didn’t rely on uniqueness to reverse; it instead held the evidence didn’t show seven multiplications. For preserving issues in patent cases tried to a jury, how specific must a Rule 50(a) motion be to avoid waiver? If a party challenges sufficiency on ‘not three unique signals’ but also argues ‘not seven multiplications,’ is it enough to preserve the latter even if the former is waived? Any guidance on how granular Rule 50(a) contentions must be in complex claim-element disputes?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit vacate the damages award rather than remand for a new damages trial?
questions.question_body: The court reversed JMOL denials on noninfringement for all asserted claims of both patents, then vacated the damages award. Is vacatur automatic whenever all liability findings are reversed, or are there scenarios where the Federal Circuit would still remand for a new damages trial (e.g., if some claims/products remained infringed)? If liability is entirely extinguished, is vacatur of damages the only proper disposition, and what happens to any ongoing royalty or future damages components in a lump-sum verdict covering the remaining patent term?
